Increasingly this will be the new job description for a lot of roles, not just coding. We’re clearly moving from a world where agents help us do our work incrementally better or faster, to us helping agents do their work.

This turns everyone in one of these positions to that of a manager of a team of agents, instead of an individual contributor with just some added leverage from AI. The biggest areas of impact will be information-heavy jobs, like coding, cybersecurity, legal work, biotech, engineering, and many other fields. 

And as a result, in these jobs your leverage will begin to be decoupled from the normal ratio of hours spent working to output generated. For essentially the history of knowledge work the main variable you had to play with was hours of work done (assuming fixed level talent/coordination/strategy). 

Now we’ve separated these variables because agents can parallelize work for us, to in theory execute as much as we need to pull off whatever goal we’re trying to accomplish. The people and organizations that discover this sooner, and orient their operations around it, will see compounding gains in their workflows.

The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. 

A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions. 

Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once. 

In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.

This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.

In AA-PersonalityBench, Kimi K3.1 Pro shows the biggest personality change we’ve seen compared to a direct predecessor

Each model is percentile ranked from 1 to 100 on each of 30 personality traits. Across all 30 traits, Kimi K3.1 Pro's ranks moved by an average of 30 points from Kimi K3's (next largest is 23, for GPT-6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol), and 18 of the 30 traits moved by 25 points or more.

We are collaborating with Silicon Data to bring market-based GPU pricing into AA-AgentPerf, our datacenter system performance benchmark

Our users and partners want to know how much agent work they can support per dollar of compute. @silicondata's rental price indices allow us to report a reliable value-for-money metric, updated daily as prices change. We currently display Silicon Data indices for H100, H200, B200 and B300, tracked across cloud providers

The new metric is Throughput per $/hr, which divides the total throughput of a system and serving configuration by the hourly cost of renting that system. Among systems with available rental pricing, NVIDIA’s B300 generally leads, while B200 matches it at faster output speeds on some models

Note: the below chart includes an MI355X rental rate that has been assumed by Artificial Analysis based on recent market quotes

Signing in to your company's plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now.

Team and Enterprise admins can set them up, and teammates are connected automatically the first time they use the plugins.

Friday was my last day at Anthropic.

Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.

When we first launched, most people approved every permission prompt by hand and mostly used Claude to answer questions and write tests. 

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

Excited to see what you all make next!

Stateless sandboxes are the wrong benchmark. Agents are only useful if they have their workspace with them (identity, skills, repos, memories…)

Vercel Sandbox team has been beautifully delivering on their latency & throughput SLOs, while prioritizing reliability and security.

Doing this while shipping clusters in 19 (‼️) global regions, new features every week, and under immense amount of customer demand in the double digit growth percentage per week.

npm i -g ai-cli 

Such a simple idea. An 𝚊𝚒 CLI. Gives every agent access to video, voice, image, text generation. And 𝚊𝚒 𝚍𝚎𝚌𝚒𝚍𝚎 brings Jev-class models.

All behind AI Gateway with cost and ZDR controls.

I've been looking forward to this day, because Vercel has an internal security agent that is **astonishingly effective** (lovingly called @𝚑𝚊𝚌𝚔𝚎𝚛). Every single line of code gets audited, automatically.

You can now get the same power. Just enable it on all your repos (this product works whether you host on Vercel or not) and your peace of mind will increase tremendously. You'll see it catch things that every other agent misses.

Why: you cannot just bank on your engineers having a skill installed, prompting "please make secure", or rolling the weights' dice that the code is good out of the gate.

The other cool thing about this is that this was entirely developed by our security team. A lot of companies out there are probably in a mad rush right now trying to staff up. If you wanted to 'download a security team' as software, this is the closest you get today.

AI agents running on employee endpoints are becoming a systemic security risk for enterprises & governments. 

Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.

In this security advisory, we outline the risks and recommend a path forward.

I always cringe a little when people refer to me as an “expert” in ai policy. This field is too new, too thinly institutionalized, too pre-paradigmatic, to have any experts at all. We are on the open seas.

The positive side of this is that the field is wide open to people looking to make novel contributions. There is no grand literature to learn, no pantheon of elders to whom one must pay their dues.

Without commenting on the Takehi et al. “Weight-Space Programming” work in particular, I do suspect that a lot of RSI (and a lot of AI-driven scientific progress more broadly) will be driven by applying what were once mundane-but-difficult techniques at a scale that would have been unimaginable when the techniques were invented.
